questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: An alliance kept credible by troops that stayed at home
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the alliance's credibility did not rest on forward troop numbers
questions.stem: Reef tank notebook, 21 May: I am writing the note for the school visit about how an alliance keeps its promise when most of its soldiers are far away. Explain why the size of the force in Europe was not the whole of the guarantee.

answer.exemplar: The treaty promised that an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, and members rightly asked what would actually happen if Soviet forces pushed into western Europe. The answer lay less in the divisions then stationed on the continent than in what could be brought: a trained reserve at home, a draft that could be enlarged, a rearmament programme, and an industrial base able to produce the equipment of war. Those who favoured a large forward force argued that a visible presence would deter; those who favoured restraint argued that a small force with a credible capacity to expand was cheaper and no less binding. The weakness of that argument lay in whether the will to expand would arrive before the front did.

questions.explanation: Credibility rested on reserves, the draft and industrial capacity at home, not on the divisions already forward. Believing a treaty text alone, or that forward numbers settled it, misses the argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the home arsenal added.

questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reasoning behind fixing the order of call by lot
questions.stem: Jellyfish column, 11 May: I am explaining to the school group why the 1940 conscription act used lots to fix the order of call. Explain the reasoning behind that arrangement.

answer.exemplar: The boards that ran the draft were local, and their members knew the men before them, so the danger was that the order of call would be arranged by friendship, by money, or by a wish to see a particular family spared. The act therefore provided that men within a district should be called in an order settled by lot, so that the sequence was the result of chance and could not be bought or argued over. Local boards still decided who was eligible, who was deferred as a father, and who was exempt, so the lot decided sequence rather than status, and the published lists allowed each man to see where he stood.

questions.explanation: The lot removed favouritism in the order of call while leaving the boards' decisions on eligibility intact. Believing it chose who served, or that it settled deferments, misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the lot decided, not what it did not.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Detention ordered without a charge
questions.learningObjective: Explain how people could be held without any charge against them
questions.stem: Riffle tank card, 22 June: I am writing the display caption on why the people sent to the camps could not simply refuse. Explain how the legal system made the order unavoidable.

answer.exemplar: The order to leave was issued under military authority to protect a designated area, and the power behind it did not depend on anyone's guilt. A person who stayed was not charged with a past offence but with disobeying the order itself, and that charge was heard by a military commission rather than an ordinary court, with the government as both prosecutor and the source of the order it prosecuted the failure to obey. Because the only crime available was resistance to the order, refusal produced the very punishment the order existed to prevent, and so the family boarded the trucks. Detention thus followed from the absence of any charge against the people themselves.

questions.explanation: The only charge was disobeying the order itself, tried by a military commission, so refusal produced punishment at the government's initiative. Believing people faced an ordinary charge misstates the mechanism.
questions.hint: Think about what the government prosecuted.

questions.stem: Plankton net tank, 9 January: I am preparing the cabinet card for the exhibit. Explain how the government and Congress between them handled the ruling.

answer.exemplar: The ruling removed the foundation on which the programme rested, because the codes had been made binding by a delegation the Court would not accept, and no appeal could restore what the Court had denied. Rather than spend a further year fighting, the administration accepted the result and looked for a legal path that survived it, and Congress supplied one: the codes lost the force of law and their presidential approval, while the prohibition on unfair methods of competition and the power of the trade commission were continued. questions.topic: A state professional school and equal protection
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism the 1896 ruling provided to opponents of separation
questions.stem: Dredge spoil tank, 17 July: I am writing the caption for the cabinet drawer on how the 1896 ruling was used for the next half century. Explain the mechanism it provided.

answer.exemplar: The ruling handed opponents of segregation a workable argument and a bad piece of law at the same time. Because separation was lawful only where the facilities were genuinely equal, the burden fell on the state to show, school by school and year by year, that a separate establishment was comparable in teachers, buildings and instruction. Every one of those terms was open to argument, and in practice a separate school could rarely be shown to be equal, so the separate school was the weaker one and the litigation mounted. The result was a decade of case-by-case decisions in which the Court upheld the separate but equal formula while probing its limits, until the argument that separate schooling was by its nature unequal carried the day and the formula was set aside.

questions.explanation: Because separation was lawful only on condition of real equality, the burden fell on the state, and each comparison produced fresh arguments, so the rule was examined case by case. Believing it settled the schools question misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask what the burden forced people to compare.

answer.exemplar: A run of that length is not a structure but a habit, and habits are made of things that happen: the same candidate, the same party, the same assumptions about the other side, and an electorate that has grown old enough to take the outcome for granted. The generation that had lived through the crash and the war had been replaced at the polls, and a party that had governed for twenty years began to be judged by what it had done rather than by what it promised. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: An alliance kept credible by troops that stayed at home
questions.learningObjective: Explain why keeping forces at home was not a dodge
questions.stem: Sponge nursery vat, 27 August: the guide asks why the argument about troops at home was not simply a way of avoiding commitment. Explain the answer given.

answer.exemplar: The argument was not a device for holding back. The commitment was judged by what could be done, and in the years after the war the United States was still reducing its forces and demobilising millions of men, so the question of whether the guarantee could be honoured was not rhetorical. A small force in Europe was defended as the visible edge of a much larger capacity: a draft that could be enlarged, divisions that could be shipped, an industrial base that could produce the equipment of war, and a reserve that could be called. The defence was that a commitment backed by these was stronger than a larger forward force that could be matched locally, and its weakness was that the will to act had to be demonstrated before it was tested.

questions.explanation: The defence was that a small forward force was the edge of a larger capacity at home, still demobilising and so to be shown rather than asserted. Believing it was a way to avoid commitment misses the reasoning.
questions.hint: Ask what was still being wound down.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Detention ordered without a charge
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the case against the removal was brought
questions.stem: Crayfish raceway, 1 February: the display panel on the appeal to justice needs a plain account of why the case was made. Explain it.

answer.exemplar: The case was made because the removal had a feature that ordinary administrative action does not usually have: it operated on people who had done nothing, and it operated on them in bulk, on the strength of a conclusion about a group rather than about any person. Once the government's own officials described the removal as an evacuation, they were describing a measure taken for reasons they were not prepared to state, and the only tribunal able to test that was a court, on a question of law rather than of policy. The absurdity the argument exposed was that a man could be imprisoned without any charge, and the only charge available against him was the failure to do as he had been told. That is what the case turned on, and it is why the legal question could be put in the simple form it took.

questions.explanation: The case rested on the absence of any individual accusation and on the fact that the only charge was disobedience of the order itself, an absurdity a court could test. Believing it rested on camp conditions misses the ground of the challenge.
questions.hint: Ask what charge was actually possible.
